assessment_summary: The statement asserts that any two connected graphs with isomorphic line graphs must be isomorphic. A proof attempt would fail when considering the well-known exception to Whitney's isomorphism theorem. Whitney's theorem guarantees this property for all graphs EXCEPT one specific pair: the complete bipartite graph K_{1,3} (the star graph with 4 vertices) and the complete graph K_3 (the triangle graph with 3 vertices). Both of these graphs have isomorphic line graphs (both line graphs are K_3). Therefore, a step assuming that a bijection between the edges of two connected graphs that preserves adjacency uniquely determines a bijection between their vertices would be unjustified, as this single counterexample breaks the implication.
counterexample: Let G1 be the star graph K_{1,3} with vertices {u, v1, v2, v3} and edges {uv1, uv2, uv3}. Let G2 be the triangle graph K_3 with vertices {a, b, c} and edges {ab, bc, ca}. Both G1 and G2 are connected graphs. The line graph L(G1) has 3 vertices (the edges of G1) which are mutually adjacent because they all share the central vertex u. Thus, L(G1) is isomorphic to K_3. The line graph L(G2) also has 3 vertices (the edges of G2) which are mutually adjacent because they share the vertices a, b, and c pairwise. Thus, L(G2) is also isomorphic to K_3. Therefore, L(G1) is isomorphic to L(G2). However, G1 and G2 are clearly not isomorphic, as G1 has 4 vertices and G2 has 3 vertices.
